Executive Summary
  • Rate hiked 25bp to 3.75–4.00% on a unanimous 12–0 vote, after holds at the April, June and July meetings; the Committee said the move will support a timelier return of inflation to 2%.
  • Hawks on board: Hammack, Kashkari and Logan, who dissented for a hike in July, voted with the majority – no dissents this time.
  • Inflation still elevated: August PCE estimated at 3.8% (core 3.4%); under the new BEA methodology due at end-September, 3.6% (core 3.2%). Unemployment fell to 4.1%.
  • More tightening likely: most participants see another increase in the target range as appropriate by year-end, data permitting.
01
Market Developments and Open Market Operations
Markets price in a September hike; yields up ~35bp, equities up, dollar weaker.
  • Resilient data with persistent inflation, geopolitical tension that pushed energy prices up, and policy communications lifted the market-implied policy path, Treasury yields, near-term inflation compensation and equities; the dollar depreciated.
  • Policy rate expectations: markets and outreach put high odds on a 25bp hike in September; the Desk survey saw a considerable probability of at least 25bp of firming by year-end, with substantial uncertainty at longer horizons.
  • Treasury yields: nominal yields rose ~35bp across the 2- to 10-year segment on a higher expected policy path and strong data; geopolitics, uncertainty around the Treasury buyback program and heavy AI-related private debt issuance also pushed term premiums up.
  • Inflation compensation: near-term measures rose, largely on oil; longer-term market and survey measures stayed consistent with 2%.
  • Equities/credit: equities rose modestly, led by AI-infrastructure beneficiaries; the year's gain is entirely earnings-driven while P/E multiples declined; hyperscaler debt spreads stayed wide.
  • Dollar: fell against major currencies on narrowing rate differentials and better foreign growth; the joint U.S.–Japan yen intervention in late July also contributed (Desk acted as Treasury's fiscal agent; the SOMA was not involved).
  • Money markets: stable, with a large increase in T-bill issuance absorbed well; reserves remain in the ample range and the Desk paused reserve management purchases, with the pace not on a preset course.
The Committee unanimously ratified the Desk's domestic transactions. There were no foreign currency interventions for the System's account.
02
Staff Review of the Economic Situation
Inflation edges up to 3.8% on energy; unemployment falls to 4.1%; growth stays solid.
PCE Estimated (Aug)
3.8% | Core: 3.4%
PCE New BEA Method (Aug)
3.6% | Core: 3.2%
Unemployment (Aug)
4.1%
Avg Hourly Earnings (Aug)
+3.1% y/y
  • Total PCE inflation edged up on a rebound in energy prices after two months of declines; core stayed at 3.4%. Staff attributes the year-on-year rise mostly to past tariffs, higher energy and input costs, and AI-related tech goods prices.
  • Under the new BEA methodology (implemented at end-September), the staff estimates August total PCE at 3.6% and core at 3.2%.
  • Unemployment moved down to 4.1% in July and August; participation stepped back up and payroll gains picked up notably in August across a range of industries. ECI (+3.3% y/y through June) and average hourly earnings were both below year-earlier levels.
  • GDP growth solid in H1, about last year's pace; private domestic final purchases picked up notably and outpaced GDP. The AI buildout fueled business investment and high-tech imports, while real energy exports hit record highs in Q2.
  • Abroad: growth stepped up in Q2 despite geopolitical tensions and high energy prices; manufacturing solid on AI-related demand; China's domestic demand weak.
  • Foreign inflation above target in many economies on energy and food; the ECB raised its policy rate and most central banks stayed focused on inflation risks.
03
Staff Review of the Financial Situation
Yields and rate expectations climb; credit stays accommodative for large firms.
  • The expected policy path and Treasury yields increased notably, driven by geopolitical news and FOMC communications amid a resilient outlook; inflation compensation explained most of the rise at shorter maturities and real rates at longer ones, with inflation compensation still consistent with a return to 2%.
  • Equities rose somewhat on robust, AI-boosted earnings; S&P 500 implied volatility ended near its historical median.
  • Abroad: policy-rate expectations in major advanced economies moved up notably with energy prices; the broad dollar index declined moderately as short-term rates rose more abroad than in the U.S.; foreign equities were mixed.
  • Short-term funding stable: the tri-party repo rate averaged 3bp below IORB and the EFFR 2bp below, even with sizable net bill issuance.
  • Credit accommodative for larger businesses and municipalities, somewhat restrictive for residential mortgage borrowers and small businesses; borrowing costs rose moderately, hyperscaler spreads edged down, and private-credit direct lending slowed in July amid subdued retail interest.
04
Staff Economic Outlook
Stronger growth and higher inflation than in July; risks to activity now roughly balanced.
  • Inflation seen declining over the rest of the year as gasoline prices ease, stepping down over the next two years as tariff, geopolitical and AI effects wane, reaching 2% in 2029; the forecast is somewhat higher for 2026–2028 than in July.
  • GDP growth seen picking up in H2 and outpacing potential through 2028 on strong business investment, solid consumer spending and supportive financial conditions; unemployment stays below its longer-run rate through 2029. The activity outlook is stronger than in July, mostly on incoming data.
  • Uncertainty remains substantial (persistent inflation, AI effects, geopolitics). Risks to employment/GDP are now roughly balanced; inflation risks remain skewed to the upside.
05
Participants' Views
All back a 25bp hike; most see another increase likely by year-end.
Inflation ↑ (Rising)
  • Inflation remained elevated and participants had not seen sufficient progress in recent months, with higher crude and fuel prices and surging AI-related investment adding pressure. Core services ex-housing and core goods stayed elevated; medium- and longer-term expectations stayed consistent with 2%.
  • Risks judged skewed to the upside, some said more so lately: the longer energy prices stay high, the greater the risk of broader price pressures.
Labor Market → (Stable)
  • Conditions stable and close to maximum employment; a majority saw the market strengthening a bit. Several noted unusually low dynamism, and AI-related skilled workers saw strong wage gains, but aggregate wage growth stayed moderate. Risks broadly balanced.
Activity ↑ (Solid)
  • Solid expansion on robust business investment and resilient consumer spending; several saw the AI buildout surprising to the upside. Low- and moderate-income households were strained by energy prices.
  • Many judged financial conditions supportive despite higher long-term yields (housing the exception). AI is expected to lift productivity over time, though timing and size are uncertain.
Monetary Policy ↑ (Hike)
  • All participants supported raising the target range 25bp to 3.75–4.00%: inflation remained elevated while labor-market risks had diminished and were broadly balanced. Many framed it as risk-management insurance against persistent inflation.
  • Most participants saw another increase as likely appropriate by year-end, with decisions data-dependent. A few asked for stronger tools to address Treasury-market stress.
18 participants submitted projections; the Summary of Economic Projections was released separately after the meeting.

Executive Summary
  • Rate held at 3.50–3.75% on a 9–3 vote; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissented, preferring a 25bp hike – the most hawkish split of the year.
  • Statement language kept: the Committee retained June's "will deliver price stability" line for a second straight meeting.
  • Inflation eased slightly: June PCE stepped down to 3.7% (core 3.3%), from May's 4.1% (core 3.4%), on lower energy prices – though risks are still seen skewed to the upside.
  • Meeting cadence floated: the Chairman raised moving to six scheduled meetings a year (from eight); no decision was made.
01
Market Developments and Open Market Operations
Mideast tensions push oil and yields up; equities dip slightly on hike odds for September.
  • Oil prices ended the period higher on escalating Middle East tensions; inflation compensation moved little despite this; nominal rates rose largely on higher policy-rate expectations; equities were somewhat lower and the dollar edged up modestly.
  • Near-term inflation compensation fell notably after the June meeting, then rose only marginally despite the oil-price jump – attributed to investor confidence in the Committee's price-stability resolve from June.
  • Treasury yields: nominal yields rose 25–30bp on higher real rates; markets priced ~1-in-3 odds of a July hike, fully pricing a 25bp hike by September and another by Q1 2027. The Desk survey median instead saw no change this year or next, but a cut in early 2028.
  • Equities/credit: the S&P 500 was down marginally; AI-infrastructure stocks have outperformed since January, though that appreciation stalled intermeeting; hyperscaler credit spreads widened further; BDC redemption requests kept rising in Q2.
  • International: U.S. policy-rate expectations rose more than in other advanced economies; resilient U.S. growth kept foreign inflows strong, especially into equities; the dollar kept appreciating.
  • Money markets: generally stable; a brief bout of repo softness dragged EFFR down 1bp temporarily before recovering. Reserves remain in the ample range.
The Committee unanimously ratified the Desk's domestic transactions. There were no foreign currency interventions.
02
Staff Review of the Economic Situation
Inflation steps down on lower energy prices; growth slows a touch but labor stays stable.
PCE Total (May)
4.1% | Core: 3.4%
PCE Estimated (Jun)
3.7% | Core: 3.3%
Unemployment (Jun)
4.2%
Avg Hourly Earnings (Jun)
+3.5% y/y (-0.4pp)
  • Core goods inflation up on tariffs and AI-related price pressures; core services edged up as firmer nonhousing services outweighed a housing slowdown.
  • Payroll growth slowed in June, though H1 average job gains stayed well above 2025's pace; unemployment at 4.2%, little changed over two years.
  • Q2 GDP growth slowed overall, though private domestic final purchases outpaced GDP; consumer spending firmed and the AI buildout kept supporting investment. Exports and imports both grew robustly on high-tech and energy trade, but net exports still subtracted from growth.
  • Abroad: growth picked up in Q2 despite commodity volatility and Middle East-linked disruptions; labor markets stable, manufacturing solid on AI-driven tech demand.
  • Foreign inflation above target in many economies on energy and food; most foreign central banks held rates steady.
03
Staff Review of the Financial Situation
Equities dip near record highs; staff still rates financial vulnerabilities "notable."
  • The policy rate path and Treasury yields moved up on FOMC communications perceived as more restrictive; real yields drove the rise. Short-term inflation compensation fell, mostly on technical factors; longer-term measures stayed anchored.
  • Equities dipped slightly but stayed near all-time highs on strong profit and risk-sentiment expectations; the VIX ticked up slightly above its historical median; corporate spreads stayed very low.
  • AFE yields rose broadly in line with the US; the dollar appreciated further, especially against AFE currencies; Korea and Taiwan equities fell on semiconductor valuation concerns.
  • Credit remained accommodative for large firms and municipalities, restrictive for small businesses and households; private credit stayed under pressure and mortgage activity remained depressed. July SLOOS showed easier standards for a 4th straight quarter and stronger demand for a 5th.
Financial Stability Assessment
  • System vulnerabilities remain rated "notable". Equity valuations stayed high on AI enthusiasm – the equity premium was at its lowest since the dot-com bubble. Hedge fund leverage sat near all-time highs, highly concentrated in the largest funds; life insurers held elevated exposure to riskier, less liquid assets. Bank capital and dealer leverage stayed healthy, though hedge funds' repo and prime brokerage borrowing hit record levels.
04
Staff Economic Outlook
Forecast little changed from June; inflation still seen near 2% by 2028.
  • Inflation seen declining in H2 as gasoline prices ease and core cools modestly; expected to step down next year as tariff/conflict effects fade, reaching ~2% in 2028 – forecast little changed from June.
  • GDP seen slightly above potential next year on financial conditions and AI investment; outlook a touch weaker than June's, mostly on incoming data. Unemployment near its longer-run rate this year, edging lower next year, ending slightly below it in 2028.
  • Uncertainty remains substantial (geopolitics, AI effects). Risks to employment/GDP skewed to the downside; inflation risks skewed to the upside, with persistence still a concern.
05
Participants' Views
Most support holding the rate; several push for a hike, judging policy not yet restrictive enough.
Inflation ↓ (Easing, still high)
  • Total PCE inflation moved down in June to 3.7% (core 3.3%), largely on a sharp drop in energy prices, but participants judged underlying pressures still broad based – core services ex-housing and AI-related items (chips, steel, electricity, software) stayed elevated. Inflation risks judged skewed to the upside amid a re-escalation of the Middle East conflict.
Labor Market → (Stable)
  • Labor demand and supply broadly balanced; unemployment near its longer-run level, payroll gains matching labor force growth. Strong AI-related demand for skilled trades (electricians, machinists, engineers) pushed up their wages, while a few participants flagged lingering softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment).
Activity ↑ (Solid)
  • Solid expansion continued despite elevated uncertainty, led by AI-related business investment and firmer consumer spending; low- and moderate-income households faced growing strain from inflation eroding real income.
Monetary Policy → (Hold)
  • Most participants supported holding the rate to gather more clarity on the inflation outlook; several favored a 25bp hike now, judging price pressures broad based and policy not yet restrictive enough.
  • The Chairman raised the idea of moving to six scheduled meetings a year (from eight), arguing it would let more information accumulate between meetings; he asked the Committee for input, but no decision was made and 2026's calendar is unaffected.

Executive Summary
  • Rate held at 3.50–3.75% on a unanimous 12–0 vote; the postmeeting statement was shortened and no longer includes the easing-bias language.
  • Leadership change: Kevin Warsh takes over as Chairman; Jerome Powell remains a voting member.
  • Inflation still rising: May PCE estimated at 4.1% (core 3.4%), up from April's 3.8% (core 3.3%), on tariffs, Middle East-linked energy costs, and the AI buildout.
  • Communications overhaul: the Chairman outlined five task forces to review the Committee's conduct of monetary policy.
01
Market Developments and Open Market Operations
Mideast optimism eases oil and inflation gauges; equities and yields still climb on AI.
  • Oil futures and near-term inflation compensation fell materially on optimism around a Middle East resolution and a US–Iran memorandum of understanding; expected policy rates, Treasury yields, the dollar, and equities all rose.
  • Policy rate expectations: markets and the Desk survey see no change in June; the median path implies no change through early 2027 and one cut in Q2 2027. Market pricing implies one hike by mid-2027, likely boosted by term premiums.
  • Treasury yields: the 10-year rose ~20bp since April and ~50bp since the conflict began; ownership has shifted somewhat toward more price-sensitive private investors.
  • Equities: the S&P 500 rose nearly 6% intermeeting, led by tech on higher earnings expectations; IPO activity is picking up to help fund AI infrastructure.
  • Private credit: BDC inflows slowed notably in Q2; net inflows likely turning more negative amid rising redemptions.
  • International: the 2-year Treasury yield rose more than similar AFE yields; the dollar appreciated modestly on widening rate differentials.
  • Money markets: generally stable, though repo rates dropped 15bp below IORB in mid-May (EFFR −2bp, the first such move since November); modest ON RRP take-up confirmed the floor held. Reserves remain in the ample range.
The Committee unanimously ratified the Desk's domestic transactions. There were no foreign currency interventions.
02
Staff Review of the Economic Situation
Inflation keeps climbing on tariffs, energy and AI demand; growth and labor stay solid.
PCE Total (Apr)
3.8% | Core: 3.3%
PCE Estimated (May)
4.1% | Core: 3.4%
Unemployment (May)
4.3%
Avg Hourly Earnings (May)
+3.4% y/y (-0.5pp)
  • Core goods inflation up on tariffs and AI-related price pressures; core services roughly stable (housing deceleration offset by firmer nonhousing services).
  • Payrolls rose at a solid pace over the three months through May; the employment cost index held at +3.4% y/y, unchanged from a year earlier.
  • Q2 GDP growth solid; private domestic final purchases outpaced GDP. The AI buildout keeps boosting investment in data centers, high-tech equipment and software; April trade showed strong high-tech goods flows and a jump in energy exports.
  • Abroad: growth stepped down in Q1 (Canada, euro area, Mexico weak); high-income Asia stayed robust on AI-driven tech exports. The conflict weighed on activity elsewhere via energy costs and weaker confidence, especially lower-income Asia and Europe.
  • Foreign inflation rose sharply on energy; the ECB and other central banks raised rates or signaled a slower pace of easing.
03
Staff Review of the Financial Situation
Stronger data lifts yields and equities; AI optimism offsets the drag from higher rates.
  • The policy rate path and Treasury yields moved higher on stronger-than-expected data; policy-path uncertainty rose, partly on a higher term premium. Short-term inflation compensation fell but stayed slightly elevated; longer-term measures remained anchored.
  • Equities rose notably on robust earnings and AI optimism despite higher yields; the VIX slipped below its historical median and corporate spreads narrowed.
  • Foreign markets moved on prospects – then confirmation – of a Strait of Hormuz reopening agreement; AFE policy expectations and inflation compensation fell, though markets still priced further hikes in the euro area and UK. The dollar rose on widening rate differentials.
  • Credit remained accommodative for large firms and municipalities, somewhat restrictive for small businesses and households. Leveraged loan issuance picked up to a robust pace, while the private credit market kept slowing.
04
Staff Economic Outlook
Inflation forecast revised up again; growth seen a touch lower than in April.
  • Inflation forecast for this year and next revised up from April on incoming data, higher energy/input costs from the conflict, and AI-buildout effects on consumer prices. Total inflation seen slowing in H2 as gasoline prices ease, though core stays little changed this year; inflation steps down next year as tariff effects wane, reaching ~2% in 2028.
  • GDP outlook a bit lower than April's, mostly on incoming data: growth near potential this year and slightly above potential over the next two years, on strong productivity, AI capex and supportive financial conditions. Unemployment stays near its longer-run rate through next year, edging down slightly in 2028.
  • Uncertainty remains elevated (Middle East conflict, AI investment/adoption effects). Risks to employment/GDP tilted somewhat to the downside; inflation risks more skewed to the upside – persistence remains the staff's most salient risk.
05
Participants' Views
All support holding the rate; the statement is shorter and drops the easing-bias language.
Inflation ↑ (Rising)
  • Inflation increased further, well above 2%, on lingering tariff effects, Strait of Hormuz-related supply disruptions, and strong AI-driven demand. Price pressures broadened (transportation, airfares, petrochemicals, agricultural inputs); services inflation excluding housing stayed high. Medium/long-term expectations still seen near 2%.
Labor Market → (Stable)
  • Unemployment stayed near its longer-run level; payroll gains roughly matched labor force growth. Other indicators (openings, claims, layoffs) pointed to a balanced but less dynamic market. Most saw the labor market as not currently a source of inflation pressure.
Activity ↑ (Solid)
  • Solid expansion despite elevated uncertainty, led by AI-related business investment and resilient consumption (helped by stock gains and tax refunds for higher-income households); lower-income households leaned more on credit amid high gas and grocery prices.
Monetary Policy → (Hold)
  • All participants supported holding the rate. Upside inflation risks stayed elevated while downside employment risks eased slightly; a few saw a case for hiking but backed holding for now. Most preferred not to repeat the easing-bias language and favored a shorter statement; the Chairman outlined five task forces to review the Committee's broader conduct of monetary policy.

Executive Summary
  • Rate held at 3.50–3.75%, with the Committee "attentive to the risks to both sides" of its dual mandate.
  • Inflation rising: March PCE estimated at 3.5% (core 3.2%), driven by energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict.
  • Growing internal split: one dissent for a 25bp cut (Miran) and three votes against the easing-bias language (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan).
  • Financial stability: staff still rates system vulnerabilities as "notable" – elevated hedge fund leverage and private credit strain.
01
Market Developments and Open Market Operations
The Mideast conflict still dominates asset prices; rates and the dollar ease after the ceasefire.
  • Equities more than reversed their earlier declines; 2- and 10-year Treasury yields rose further; the dollar retraced part of its earlier appreciation.
  • Oil: futures curve higher than in March, though its forecasting record is mixed.
  • Inflation expectations: near-term expectations rose again; longer-term measures remain anchored near 2%.
  • Policy rate expectations: markets see little change this year; options imply ~30% odds of a hike by Q1 2027. The Desk survey points to two 25bp cuts, but later than before (Q3/Q4 2026 and Q1 2027).
  • Private credit: signs of stabilization despite continued redemptions.
  • Money markets: conditions stable; reserves remain in the ample range.
  • Swap lines: unanimous renewal with Canada, the UK, Japan, the ECB and Switzerland, plus the North American Framework with Mexico and Canada.
The Committee unanimously ratified the Desk's domestic transactions. There were no foreign currency interventions.
02
Staff Review of the Economic Situation
Inflation elevated on energy prices; labor market stable but soft; GDP rebounds in Q1.
PCE Total (Feb)
2.8% | Core: 3.0%
PCE Estimated (Mar)
3.5% | Core: 3.2%
Unemployment (Mar)
4.3%
Avg Hourly Earnings (Mar)
+3.5% y/y (-0.7pp)
  • Core goods prices rose on tariffs; core services eased as housing costs slowed.
  • Payrolls rebounded in March after February's drop (health-care strike and harsh weather); on average, job gains stayed low.
  • Q1 GDP picked up as shutdown effects faded; net exports were a significant drag (tech imports rose more than exports).
  • Abroad: Asia and China solid; Mexico weak on autos; European and Asian firms report longer delivery times and higher input costs from the conflict.
  • Foreign inflation rising on energy; only Banxico cut its rate (-25bp).
03
Staff Review of the Financial Situation
Markets resilient despite the conflict; financial vulnerabilities remain "notable."
  • The implied policy rate path rose modestly on conflict-related inflation concerns.
  • Equities rose despite geopolitical volatility, supported by solid earnings; corporate spreads tightened.
  • Foreign markets swung sharply; sentiment improved after the ceasefire, weighing on the dollar.
  • Credit conditions restrictive for small businesses and households; accommodative for large firms and municipalities.
  • April SLOOS: further easing in lending standards, especially for consumer loans.
Financial Stability Assessment
  • System vulnerabilities remain rated "notable": housing valuations near historic highs, elevated leverage at hedge funds (Treasury trades) and life insurers. Bank capital ratios remain high historically, though market-adjusted ratios have declined. Funding risk is moderate (low reliance on uninsured deposits).
04
Staff Economic Outlook
Growth a bit stronger than in March; inflation rises this year, returns to ~2% by late 2027.
  • Real GDP projected slightly above potential, supported by favorable financial conditions and AI-related capital spending. Unemployment near its longer-run rate through 2027, edging down slightly in 2028.
  • This year's inflation forecast revised up on the conflict and energy prices, with disinflation expected after H1.
  • Uncertainty remains elevated (conflict plus AI adoption). Downside risks to employment/GDP; upside risks to inflation – persistence is the staff's most salient risk.
05
Participants' Views
Nearly all favor holding the rate; many wanted to drop the easing-bias language.
Inflation ↑ (Rising)
  • Headline and core above 2%. Participants cited tariffs, shipping/airfares, fertilizer, and tech/software prices. Long-term expectations stable; near-term expectations up.
Labor Market → (Stable)
  • Most see stabilization, though some flag fragility (sector concentration, lower job availability). Risks skewed to the downside on a possible hiring pullback (uncertainty, AI).
Activity ↑ (Solid)
  • Solid expansion, strong tech investment, resilient consumption but weak sentiment. Agriculture pressured by fuel and fertilizer costs.
Financial Stability ⚠ (Elevated)
  • Concerns over private credit, hedge fund leverage, and cybersecurity (tied to AI).
Monetary Policy → (Hold)
  • Nearly all supported holding the rate. Many would have dropped the easing-bias language; one participant preferred a 25bp cut on employment risks.

Manual de actualización
Cómo agregar una nueva reunión FOMC al tracker
1.
Tras cada reunión del FOMC, entra a www.federalreserve.gov y descarga las FOMC Minutes en PDF, en la sección "Meeting calendars, statements, and minutes".
2.
Guarda el PDF en: W:\4. Informes\–– Informes Mensuales\Fed Meetings\Minutas Fed, con el formato de nombre AAMMDD_FOMC_Minutes.pdf (ej. 260916_FOMC_Minutes.pdf).
3.
Adjunta ese PDF aquí mismo, en este proyecto de Claude, y pídele que agregue la nueva reunión al tracker. Claude arma el panel nuevo con las 6 secciones, el resumen ejecutivo y el botón del PDF.
4.
Descarga el HTML actualizado que Claude te entregue y guárdalo (reemplazando el anterior) en: G:\Unidades compartidas\MFO-Dashboards\Monitores\Estrategia.
El tracker se actualiza reunión por reunión – hay 8 reuniones FOMC al año. Mantén siempre el formato AAMMDD_ en el nombre del PDF: la fecha define a qué reunión se asigna.
